paras: The Dixon account of political intimidation in Yazoo was a disputed report, carried by Northern Republican newspapers in August 1880, that white Democrats in Yazoo County, Mississippi, had warned F. P. Dixon against supporting James A. Garfield and were breaking up gatherings of Black men to stop political talk. Dixon was the brother of H. M. Dixon, whose earlier killing in Yazoo was blamed on James Barksdale. Governor J. M. Stone, Yazoo City officials and the editors of the Yazoo Herald denied the account as false, and no violence during the visit was reported by either side.

Republican papers described H. M. Dixon, also called "Col. Dixon," as murdered in Yazoo County by Barksdale, variously "last year," "two years ago" or "about a year since." They said he was killed because he ran as an independent candidate against the Democratic nominee, the Ashtabula Weekly Telegraph specifying the office of sheriff. Governor Stone instead wrote that Barksdale killed him "on account of a gross personal affront."

According to a Washington dispatch dated July 25, F. P. Dixon went to Yazoo City to see his brother's widow, who had died of "a broken heart" before he arrived, and stayed a few days. The dispatch said he had been driven out of the state after his brother's killing and warned that death awaited him if he returned. When he told acquaintances he backed Garfield, they said they would not tolerate such talk in Yazoo and advised him to go back to Washington.

The same account said the Yazoo Herald told him editorially that such opinions were not wanted, and that Nathaniel Ingraham, a farmer about three miles up the river, warned him during a social call. Ingraham was quoted as saying, "We don't intend that any votes shall be cast for Garfield here, and if you feel as you talk you had better return to the North." Dixon also said that half a dozen colored men could not gather in the street without white Democrats interrupting to forbid them to discuss politics or mention the Republican ticket. A Chicago Tribune version gave the number as five and added that no Garfield meetings would be permitted in the county.

On August 4 the Jackson Weekly Clarion reported that the Yazoo Herald "contradicts in detail" Dixon's stories and that he had been treated with civility and kindness. After the Portland Oregonian reprinted the interview from the Chicago Times, Sidney Dell of Portland wrote to Governor Stone, who replied on August 24 that he believed it "a fabrication from beginning to end" and referred the matter to Col. Garrett Andrews of Yazoo City.

Andrews wrote that no threats were made, that Dixon was never driven away, and that the Herald had printed only a one-line notice of his visit. He called the claim about colored men "the greatest falshood of all," saying hundreds of them crowded the streets daily, and added that anyone "may vote for Garfield as freely as you may in Oregon." Mayor J. H. Holt, the heads of the board of trade, bank and board of supervisors, and Herald editors J. S. McCullum and R. Walpole signed a certificate that the interview was "false, and wholly without foundation or pretext."

Republican papers in Maine, Wisconsin, Ohio, Kansas and Maryland ran the story as campaign material, under headlines such as "The Yazoo Buildozers" and "Yazoo Solid for Hancock." The Portland Daily Press set it beside cases from Texas and South Carolina under the ironic heading "A Pure Ballot," and the Emporia News linked Barksdale's role as a Hancock delegate to the brother's "foul assassination." Later in August a Chicago Tribune editorial listed Yazoo among the places where "actual bloodshed is used" when other methods fail.

Democratic papers answered in kind: the Weekly Clarion dismissed "fanciful stories retailed for Radical consumption," and the Albany, Oregon, State Rights Democrat printed the Dell, Stone and Andrews letters as "Northern Slanders of the South. A Complete Refutation." Both sides wrote about Yazoo's Black residents without quoting any of them.
Whether Dixon was threatened at all rests on his own second-hand account against the denials of the Herald, Andrews and Stone, none of it sworn.

accounts.label: Gov. J. M. Stone
accounts.gist: Stone did not know what was said to Dixon but called the account a fabrication, and said H. M. Dixon was killed over a personal affront, not by 'the Democrats of Yazoo county.'

framing.detail: Republican papers headlined it 'The Yazoo Buildozers' and 'Yazoo Solid for Hancock' and used it as campaign evidence against the Democrats.
The Emporia News called the brother's killing a 'foul assassination' that 'cries to heaven for vengeance' and tied Barksdale to Hancock's nomination.
The Portland Daily Press set the story beside Texas and South Carolina under the ironic heading 'A Pure Ballot.'
The Weekly Clarion called the account 'fanciful stories retailed for Radical consumption.'
The State Rights Democrat ran the rebuttals as 'Northern Slanders of the South. A Complete Refutation.'
